{{Short description|Mathematical property}}
{{About|mathematical use|the philosophical reduction thinking|Reduction (philosophy)}}

In mathematics, '''semi-simplicity''' is a widespread concept in disciplines such as [[linear algebra]], [[abstract algebra]], [[representation theory]], [[category theory]], and [[algebraic geometry]]. A '''semi-simple object''' is one that can be decomposed into a sum of [[Simple (abstract algebra)|simple objects]], and simple objects are those that do not contain non-trivial proper sub-objects. The precise definitions of these words depends on the context.

For example, if ''G'' is a [[finite group|finite]] [[group (mathematics)|group]], then a nontrivial finite-dimensional [[group representation|representation]] ''V'' over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] is said to be ''simple'' if the only subrepresentations it contains are either {0} or ''V'' (these are also called [[irreducible representation]]s). Now [[Maschke's theorem]] says that any finite-dimensional representation of a finite group is a direct sum of simple representations (provided the [[characteristic (field)|characteristic]] of the base field does not divide the order of the group). So in the case of finite groups with this condition, every finite-dimensional representation  is semi-simple. Especially in algebra and representation theory, "semi-simplicity" is also called '''complete reducibility'''. For example, [[Weyl's theorem on complete reducibility]] says a finite-dimensional representation of a [[semisimple Lie group|semisimple]] [[compact space|compact]] [[Lie group]] is semisimple.

A [[square matrix]] (in other words a [[linear operator]] <math>T:V \to V</math> with ''V'' a finite-dimensional vector space) is said to be ''simple'' if its only [[invariant subspace|invariant]] [[linear subspace]]s under ''T'' are {0} and ''V''. If the field is [[Algebraically closed field|algebraically closed]] (such as the [[complex number]]s), then the only simple matrices are of size 1-by-1. A ''semi-simple matrix'' is one that is [[Matrix similarity|similar]] to a [[Direct sum of matrices|direct sum]] of simple matrices; if the field is algebraically closed, this is the same as being [[Diagonalizable matrix|diagonalizable]].

These notions of semi-simplicity can be unified using the language of [[semisimple module|semi-simple]] [[Module (mathematics)|modules]], and generalized to semi-simple [[Category (mathematics)|categories]].

==Introductory example of vector spaces==
If one considers all [[vector space]]s (over a [[field (mathematics)|field]], such as the [[real number]]s), the simple vector spaces are those that contain no proper nontrivial subspaces. Therefore, the one-[[dimension (linear algebra)|dimensional]] vector spaces are the simple ones. So it is a basic result of linear algebra that any finite-dimensional vector space is the [[Direct sum of modules|direct sum]] of simple vector spaces; in other words, all finite-dimensional vector spaces are semi-simple.

==Semi-simple matrices==
A [[square matrix]] or, equivalently, a [[linear operator]] ''T'' on a finite-dimensional [[vector space]] ''V'' is called ''semi-simple'' if every ''T''-[[invariant subspace]] has a [[Direct sum of modules#Internal direct sum|complementary]] ''T''-invariant subspace.<ref name="Lam-2001-p39">Lam (2001), [{{Google books|plainurl=y|id=f15FyZuZ3-4C|page=39|text=linear operator}} p. 39]</ref><ref>{{cite book
 | last1 = Hoffman | first1 = Kenneth
 | last2 = Kunze | first2 = Ray | author2-link = Ray Kunze
 | chapter = Semi-Simple operators
 | edition = 2nd
 | location = Englewood Cliffs, N.J.
 | mr = 0276251
 | publisher = Prentice-Hall, Inc.
 | title = Linear algebra
 | url = https://archive.org/details/linearalgebra00hoff_0 | url-access = registration | year = 1971| isbn = 9780135367971
 }}</ref>  This is equivalent to the [[minimal polynomial (linear algebra)|minimal polynomial]] of ''T'' being square-free.

For vector spaces over an [[algebraically closed]] field ''F'', semi-simplicity of a matrix is equivalent to [[diagonalizable|diagonalizability]].<ref name="Lam-2001-p39"/> This is because such an operator always has an eigenvector; if it is, in addition, semi-simple, then it has a complementary invariant [[hyperplane]], which itself has an eigenvector, and thus by induction is diagonalizable. Conversely, diagonalizable operators are easily seen to be semi-simple, as invariant subspaces are direct sums of eigenspaces, and any eigenbasis for this subspace can be extended to an eigenbasis of the full space.

==Semi-simple modules and rings==
{{Further|Semisimple module|Semisimple ring}}
For a fixed [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] ''R'', a nontrivial ''R''-module ''M'' is simple, if it has no submodules other than 0 and ''M''. An ''R''-module ''M'' is [[semi-simple module|semi-simple]] if every ''R''-submodule of ''M'' is an ''R''-module direct summand of ''M'' (the trivial module 0 is semi-simple, but not simple). For an ''R''-module ''M'', ''M'' is semi-simple if and only if it is the direct sum of simple modules (the trivial module is the empty direct sum).  Finally, ''R'' is called a [[semi-simple ring]] if it is semi-simple as an ''R''-module. As it turns out, this is equivalent to requiring that any [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]] ''R''-module ''M'' is semi-simple.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Lam|first1=Tsit-Yuen|author-link=Tsit Yuen Lam|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f15FyZuZ3-4C&q=semi-simple|title=A first course in noncommutative rings|publisher=Springer|year=2001|isbn=0-387-95183-0|edition=2|series=Graduate texts in mathematics|volume=131|pages=27}} "(2.5) Theorem and Definition"</ref>

Examples of semi-simple rings include fields and, more generally, finite direct products of fields. For a finite group ''G'' [[Maschke's theorem]] asserts that the [[group ring]] ''R''[''G''] over some ring ''R'' is semi-simple if and only if ''R'' is semi-simple and |''G''| is invertible in ''R''. Since the theory of modules of ''R''[''G''] is the same as the [[representation theory]] of ''G'' on ''R''-modules, this fact is an important dichotomy, which causes [[modular representation theory]], i.e., the case when |''G''| ''does'' divide the [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] of ''R'' to be more difficult than the case when |''G''| does not divide the characteristic, in particular if ''R'' is a field of characteristic zero.
By the [[Artin–Wedderburn theorem]], a unital [[Artinian ring]] ''R'' is semisimple if and only if it is (isomorphic to) <math>M_{n_1}(D_1) \times M_{n_2}(D_2) \times \cdots \times M_{n_r}(D_r)</math>, where each <math>D_i</math> is a [[division ring]] and <math>M_n(D)</math> is the ring of ''n''-by-''n'' matrices with entries in ''D''.

An operator ''T'' is semi-simple in the sense above if and only if the subalgebra <math>F[T] \subseteq \operatorname{End}_F(V)</math> generated by the powers (i.e., iterations) of ''T'' inside the ring of [[endomorphism]]s of ''V'' is semi-simple.

As indicated above, the theory of semi-simple rings is much more easy than the one of general rings. For example, any [[short exact sequence]]
:<math>0 \to M' \to M \to M'' \to 0</math>
of modules over a semi-simple ring must split, i.e., <math>M \cong M' \oplus M''</math>. From the point of view of [[homological algebra]], this means that there are no non-trivial [[Ext functor|extension]]s. The ring '''Z''' of integers is not semi-simple: '''Z''' is not the direct sum of ''n'''''Z''' and '''Z'''/''n''.

==Semi-simple categories==
Many of the above notions of semi-simplicity are recovered by the concept of a ''semi-simple'' category ''C''. Briefly, a [[category (mathematics)|category]] is a collection of objects and maps between such objects, the idea being that the maps between the objects preserve some structure inherent in these objects. For example, ''R''-modules and ''R''-linear maps between them form a category, for any ring ''R''.

An [[abelian category]]<ref>More generally, the same definition of semi-simplicity works for [[pseudo-abelian category|pseudo-abelian]] [[additive category|additive categories]]. See for example Yves André, Bruno Kahn: ''Nilpotence, radicaux et structures monoïdales. With an appendix by Peter O'Sullivan''.  Rend. Sem. Mat. Univ. Padova  108  (2002), 107–291. https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0203273.</ref> ''C'' is called semi-simple if there is a collection of simple objects <math>X_\alpha \in C</math>, i.e., ones with no [[subobject]] other than the [[zero object]] 0 and <math>X_\alpha</math> itself, such that ''any'' object ''X'' is the [[direct sum]] (i.e., [[coproduct]] or, equivalently, product) of finitely many simple objects. It follows from [[Schur's lemma]] that the [[endomorphism ring]]
:<math displaystyle="block">\operatorname{End}_C(X)=\operatorname{Hom}_C(X, X)</math>
in a semi-simple category is a product of matrix rings over division rings, i.e., semi-simple.

Moreover, a ring ''R'' is semi-simple if and only if the category of finitely generated ''R''-modules is semisimple.

An example from [[Hodge theory]] is the category of ''polarizable pure [[Hodge structure]]s'', i.e., pure Hodge structures equipped with a suitable [[Positive-definite bilinear form|positive definite]] [[bilinear form]]. The presence of this so-called polarization causes the category of polarizable Hodge structures to be semi-simple.<ref>Peters, Chris A. M.; Steenbrink, Joseph H. M. ''Mixed Hodge structures''. Ergebnisse der Mathematik und ihrer Grenzgebiete. 3. Folge. A Series of Modern Surveys in Mathematics [Results in Mathematics and Related Areas. 3rd Series. A Series of Modern Surveys in Mathematics], 52. Springer-Verlag, Berlin, 2008. xiv+470 pp. {{isbn|978-3-540-77015-2}}; see Corollary 2.12</ref>
Another example from algebraic geometry is the category of ''pure [[motive (mathematics)|motives]]'' of [[smooth morphism|smooth]] [[projective variety|projective varieties]] over a field ''k'' <math>\operatorname{Mot}(k)_\sim</math> modulo an [[adequate equivalence relation]] <math>\sim</math>. As was conjectured by [[Alexandre Grothendieck|Grothendieck]] and shown by [[Uwe Jannsen|Jannsen]], this category is semi-simple if and only if the equivalence relation is [[numerical equivalence]].<ref>Uwe Jannsen: ''[https://epub.uni-regensburg.de/26642/1/jannsen10.pdf Motives, numerical equivalence, and semi-simplicity]'', Invent. math. 107, 447~452 (1992)</ref> This fact is a conceptual cornerstone in the theory of motives.

Semisimple abelian categories also arise from a combination of a [[t-structure|''t''-structure]] and a (suitably related) [[weight structure]] on a [[triangulated category]].<ref>{{citation |last=Bondarko|first=Mikhail V. |title=Weight structures and 'weights' on the hearts of ''t''-structures |journal=Homology Homotopy Appl.|volume=14|issue=1 |pages=239–261|year=2012|doi=10.4310/HHA.2012.v14.n1.a12|zbl=1251.18006|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Semi-simplicity in representation theory ==
{{Main|Semisimple representation}}
{{See also|Maschke's theorem|Weyl's theorem on complete reducibility}}

One can ask whether the [[category of representations|category of finite-dimensional representations]] of a group or a Lie algebra is semisimple, that is, whether every finite-dimensional representation decomposes as a direct sum of irreducible representations. The answer, in general, is no. For example, the representation of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> given by
:<math>\Pi(x)=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x\\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}
</math>
is not a direct sum of irreducibles.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Example 4.25</ref> (There is precisely one nontrivial invariant subspace, the span of the first basis element, <math>e_1</math>.) On the other hand, if <math>G</math> is [[compact group|compact]], then every finite-dimensional representation <math>\Pi</math> of <math>G</math> admits an [[inner product]] with respect to which <math>\Pi</math> is unitary, showing that <math>\Pi</math> decomposes as a sum of irreducibles.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Theorem 4.28</ref> Similarly, if <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is a complex semisimple Lie algebra, every finite-dimensional representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is a sum of irreducibles.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Theorem 10.9</ref> Weyl's original proof of this used the [[unitarian trick]]: Every such <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is the complexification of the Lie algebra of a [[simply connected]] compact Lie group <math>K</math>. Since <math>K</math> is simply connected, there is a one-to-one correspondence between the finite-dimensional representations of <math>K</math> and of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Theorem 5.6</ref> Thus, the just-mentioned result about representations of compact groups applies. It is also possible to prove semisimplicity of representations of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> directly by algebraic means, as in Section 10.3 of Hall's book.

See also: [[Fusion category]] (which are semisimple).

*A [[semisimple algebraic group]] is a linear algebraic group whose radical of the identity component is trivial.
